Words | Er Mu

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

In range, the piano is the undisputed king of instruments. But if it’s history you’re comparing, the woodwinds are the pharaohs: the earliest instruments humans invented and played. The oldest woodwind found so far dates back 40,000 years and was made by boring holes in an animal’s leg bone. (That primitive! That brutal! That hardcore!)

“Woodwind instruments include the flute, piccolo, recorder, oboe, clarinet, panpipes and bassoon, all of which have a hollow tube through which air is blown. Woodwinds take their name from the fact that they were all originally made of wood, although many are now made of metal or plastic. Woodwinds have a very long history; the primitive flutes that ancient humans made by boring holes in animal leg bones are, broadly speaking, their ancestors. Modern woodwinds developed from instruments used in folk music around the world, such as reed pipes and various transverse and end-blown flutes.”

Depending on whether they have a reed, and how many, woodwinds fall into three main groups:

Edge-tone instruments (no reed, sometimes called “air-reed” instruments): flute, piccolo, recorder, Japanese shakuhachi, Chinese dizi;

Top: flute. Bottom: piccolo.

a: recorder; b: Japanese shakuhachi; c: dizi; d: panpipes; e: ocarina

Single-reed instruments: clarinet, saxophone

Left: clarinet. Right: saxophone.

Double-reed instruments: oboe, bassoon, English horn

In this article, we’ll start with the flute and look at how the reedless edge-tone woodwinds produce their strings of lovely notes.

The flute shown above has three main parts: the head joint, the body (or middle joint) and the foot joint. The section on the far left, with the embouchure hole, is the head joint. The middle section, with its closely spaced tone holes and linked keys, is the body. The section on the far right, with a few widely spaced keys, is the foot joint. When we play, we blow across the embouchure hole while using different fingerings to open different tone holes in turn, and out come pleasing, harmonious notes. Why is that?

In our earlier article on how we produce speech sounds, we mentioned that the vocal tract can be simplified into an equivalent “source–filter” model. The flute, being a much more regular tube, is even easier to understand from the same angle.

The source: an oscillating air jet

When you play the flute, a steady jet of air leaves your mouth, heads for the embouchure hole and interacts with the far edge of the hole, the one away from your lips. When this jet is disturbed, its direction shifts and swings back and forth, now blowing into the bore of the flute, now blowing outside it, as shown below:

So what disturbs the jet and sets it swinging? None other than the vibration of the air inside the bore. That vibration makes the air near the embouchure hole move back and forth, which in turn makes the jet oscillate. The frequency at which the jet oscillates depends on the speed of the jet and on the distance from the lips to the embouchure hole: the faster the jet, and the closer the lips are to the hole, the higher the oscillation frequency.

The filter: a pipe open at both ends

The flute is really a pipe open at both ends. One opening is at the foot; the other is, in fact, the embouchure hole. Watch a flutist closely and you’ll see that the embouchure hole is never completely covered; part of it stays open to the outside air. To make things easier to explain, we need to simplify the flute further. Assume all the tone holes along the body and foot joint are closed, and move the embouchure opening in the head joint to the very end. The flute then becomes a uniform cylindrical pipe open at both ends, as shown below:

In the previous section, we said that what sets the jet oscillating is the vibration of the air in the pipe. The air in the pipe vibrates, in turn, because of the pipe’s resonances.

With the boundary conditions at both ends fixed, solving the one-dimensional wave equation readily gives the solutions for sound propagating in the pipe (standing waves), and the frequency of each solution is one of the resonance frequencies. Of course, I won’t explain it that way here; I’ll try to keep things as simple and accessible as I can.

Because the pipe is open at both ends, the air pressure at the ends must be roughly equal to atmospheric pressure. In other words, the sound pressure (the fluctuation about atmospheric pressure) there is zero. These points of zero sound pressure are called pressure nodes. They usually lie a short distance out from the center of each open end (about 0.6 times the pipe radius; this distance is known as the end correction). Inside the pipe, the pressure need not equal atmospheric pressure, so the sound pressure need not be zero. For the first standing-wave mode, the sound pressure is greatest in the middle of the pipe, a point called the pressure antinode, as shown below:

The first standing-wave mode in the pipe

The thick line in the second row shows how the sound pressure is distributed along the pipe, and the thin line in the third row shows the distribution of the particle velocity of the air. Note that the particle velocity has two antinodes, one at each end of the pipe, meaning that air can move freely in and out at both ends. (Pressure nodes and particle-velocity nodes are not the same thing. In general, a pressure node corresponds to a particle-velocity antinode, and a pressure antinode to a particle-velocity node.)

The figure above shows the standing wave with the longest wavelength that satisfies the condition of zero sound pressure at both open ends. It’s easy to see that this wavelength, λ, equals twice the pipe length, L. The frequency of this standing wave corresponds to the lowest note the flute can play: C4. (If you own a flute, measure its length with a ruler and work it out yourself with the formula f=343/2L. Does it come out close to C4, at about 262 Hz? It won’t match exactly; this is, after all, an estimate based on a simplified model.)

With all the tone holes closed, you can play not only C4 but also higher notes, just by changing how fast you blow. Why? Mainly because more standing waves also satisfy the condition of zero sound pressure at both ends, as shown below:

The pitches of the standing waves at frequencies f0, 2f0, 3f0 and so on are shown below:

Each of these standing waves corresponds to a sine wave. Played softly (pianissimo), the flute sounds pure, much like a sine tone; the harder you blow, the richer and less pure the sound becomes. This is mainly because blowing harder excites more of the standing waves. In fact, when the flute plays C4, the sound also contains other, higher notes: C4 (f0), C5 (2f0), G4 (3f0), C6 (4f0) and so on. These higher components are an important factor in the flute’s timbre (along with others, such as the temporal envelope).

Measured spectrum of a flute playing C4

To sum up

The frequency of the oscillating jet, the source, depends on the jet speed and on the distance from the lips to the embouchure hole. The flute’s bore, the filter, has a series of resonance frequencies in simple whole-number ratios. When the frequency of the jet matches one of these resonance frequencies, the flute sounds the note whose pitch corresponds mainly to that frequency. When you play, the different keys and fingerings are really changing the resonance frequencies of the pipe.

References

“The acoustics of woodwind musical instruments”, Joe Wolfe
